label: Person
name: Yakov Malik
summary:
Yakov Aleksandrovich Malik (1906–1980) was a pivotal Soviet diplomat whose career spanned the most intense phases of the Cold War, from its nascent ideological clashes to periods of détente. As the Soviet Union's Permanent Representative to the United Nations during two critical periods (1948–1952 and 1967–1976) and Ambassador to the United Kingdom (1953–1960), Malik became a globally recognized face of Soviet foreign policy. His actions on the international stage, particularly his controversial walkout from the UN Security Council in 1950, directly influenced the trajectory of the Korean War and underscored the deepening schism between East and West, making him a central figure in 20th-century diplomatic history.

Malik's diplomatic career began in the late 1930s, gaining prominence with his appointment to the United Nations shortly after its inception. He is most infamously remembered for his decision on January 13, 1950, to boycott the UN Security Council in protest over the refusal to seat the People's Republic of China, which inadvertently cleared the path for the UN's intervention in the Korean War. His absence meant the Soviet Union could not exercise its veto when the Security Council voted on June 27, 1950, to authorize military assistance to South Korea. Later, in 1951, Malik played a crucial role in initiating the armistice negotiations for the Korean War, publicly stating on June 23 that a ceasefire and armistice were possible. His tenure as Ambassador to the UK coincided with a post-Stalin thawing of relations, while his second UN appointment saw him navigate the complexities of the Vietnam War, the Arab-Israeli conflict, and the nascent era of nuclear arms control.

effects: Malik's 1950 UN Security Council walkout enabled the passage of resolutions authorizing UN intervention in the Korean War.
